captions.instagram:
How does a quartz watch work?

A sliver of quartz shaped like a tuning fork rings 32,768 times a second. A chip halves that beat fifteen times, and a magnet smaller than a grain of rice flips once a second. Take a quartz watch apart in 3D and see why it beats a mechanical watch a hundred times its price.

→ A quartz watch is a cell, a crystal, a chip, a tiny motor and a few gears.
→ Quartz is piezoelectric: bend it and it makes a voltage, give it a voltage and it bends.
→ Cut as a tiny tuning fork, it rings 32,768 times a second. This is 27,000 times slower.
→ Inside the chip, fifteen flip-flops each halve the beat: 32,768, 16,384, 8,192 …
→ … down to 4, 2, and exactly one pulse a second for the motor.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/quartzclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a quartz watch work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A sliver of quartz shaped like a tuning fork rings 32,768 times a second. A chip halves that beat fifteen times, and a magnet smaller than a grain of rice flips once a second. Take a quartz watch apart in 3D and see why it beats a mechanical watch a hundred times its price.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/quartzclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/quartzclear

In this video:
• A cell, a crystal, a chip, a motor and gears. An analog quartz watch has a silver-oxide button cell, a quartz crystal sealed in a tiny can, a chip, a coil with a flat iron stator, a magnet rotor, and a train of gears that turns the hands.
• A crystal that rings. Quartz is piezoelectric: bend it and it makes a voltage, give it a voltage and it bends.
• Halving, fifteen times. 32,768 is 2 multiplied by itself 15 times.
• A motor that moves in ticks. Each second the chip sends a pulse a few thousandths of a second long through the coil.
• Gears do the arithmetic. The rotor makes 30 turns a minute.
• Seconds a month, not seconds a day. An ordinary quartz watch is rated to about 15 seconds a month, where a certified mechanical chronometer may drift 6 seconds a day.
